summary:
Ayacucho stands under Peru's national framework. No department-specific trans statute, ordinance, enforcement action or incident series for Ayacucho appears in the sources; all attached material is national in scope, so the operative facts for a visitor to the region are the national ones.

On public-restroom access, the point at which the sources most directly address the region, Ayacucho has no separate provision, enforcement action or incident. The national restriction governs the department: on 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved, exempting it from a second vote, a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow listed exceptions. The IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 April 2025) argues this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

The legislative history is documented by Infobae Perú (20 February 2025): the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion (dictamen) merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

National hate-violence data, which the regional assessment relies on, is recorded by Agencia Presentes (22 July 2024) covering the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report: 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty (multiple gunshots, stabbings); the 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination (61 denuncias in 2020). The report recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. These are national figures with no Ayacucho-specific finding; they are raw counts without a population denominator, so they indicate national pattern rather than regional magnitude.
tangentialFactors: The sources contain no Ayacucho-specific turbulence, comparison or adjacent-risk material. The national context carried by the parent record includes the 2025 bathroom restriction's origins in a social-media complaint about airport signage, the IDEHPUCP constitutional challenge, and national hate-crime statistics; none of these is documented as occurring in or being enforced differently within Ayacucho.
localsOnly: No resident-facing facts specific to Ayacucho appear in the sources. Trans residents of the department stand under the national rules on legal name change, gender-marker change, health-insurance classification and restroom access, all of which are carried by the parent record.
outOfScopeNotes: Whether the national restroom restriction has been enforced in Ayacucho, and whether any local authority or security personnel there has applied it, is unresolved in the sources. No local court, police or municipal action on trans issues in Ayacucho is documented. The national hate-crime and homicide figures are raw counts for Peru as a whole with no department-level breakdown and no per-capita denominator, so they cannot be read as an Ayacucho-specific risk level.
